analysis.one_liner: Tests charging Medicare and Medicaid patients the lowest drug price paid in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: A single House member's bill to test lower 'most-favored-nation' drug prices for Medicare and Medicaid has no cosponsors and no committee action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government's Medicare payment-testing center to run a five-year 'most-favored-nation' model starting in 2029: drug makers would have to sell covered drugs to Medicare and Medicaid patients at the second-lowest price those drugs command in eight other wealthy countries, after rebates. Manufacturers could avoid the automatic model by signing a negotiated agreement with the Health Secretary that provides the same price access and commits to expanding US manufacturing — including agreements already struck before the bill passes. It was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors and sent to two committees, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries who fill prescriptions or receive doctor-administered drugs covered by the model. They would get access to the most-favored-nation price — the second-lowest net price across eight reference countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the UK — and Medicare and Medicaid programs would pay less for those drugs [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Starting January 1, 2029, drug makers without an agreement must give Medicare and Medicaid patients access to the most-favored-nation price for every covered drug sold in two or more reference countries, for a five-year test period [S2].

The reference price is the second-lowest average net price — accounting for all rebates and discounts — that a drug commands across Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Switzerland, and the UK, adjusted for purchasing power [S2].

The model covers all three major channels: pharmacy-dispensed drugs for Medicaid and Medicare Part D patients, and Part B drugs furnished by hospitals and physicians, so it reaches both retail prescriptions and infused or injected drugs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the cost, in the form of lower US net prices on covered drugs sold to Medicare and Medicaid patients, unless they negotiate a covered agreement — which itself requires giving up the same price access plus commitments to expand US manufacturing [S2]. Lower manufacturer revenue could mean less money available for developing new drugs, a cost industry would pass along to future patients.

drawbacks.text: The model only reaches Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries. Americans with employer or marketplace insurance — the majority of the under-65 population — get no price benefit from this bill [S2].

Manufacturers can escape the mandatory model through a 'covered agreement' with the Secretary, and the bill explicitly accommodates agreements signed before enactment; that negotiated path is where the Secretary's discretion lives, so the automatic price guarantee can be narrowed deal by deal [S2].
The Secretary may suspend the requirement for any drug if a manufacturer appears likely to sign an agreement, creating an additional off-ramp before the model even starts [S2].

Linking US prices to the second-lowest foreign net price reduces revenue on the affected drugs, which manufacturers and some economists argue would shrink investment in new drug development — a cost borne by future patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine, if narrow, price cut for Medicare and Medicaid patients on a defined list of drugs, and its weakest points are design choices an honest supporter would admit: it starts four years out, it never touches the commercial insurance market, and the covered-agreement and suspension provisions give manufacturers and the Secretary multiple ways to soften the guarantee. As a five-year demonstration rather than a permanent policy, its effects would be real but limited, and the bill as written is more of a floor than a hard price cap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in March 2026, and with no cosponsors and no committee action since, it is sitting still while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Meuser introduced the Most Favored Patient Act of 2026 in the House on March 5, 2026 [S1].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and also to the Ways and Means Committee [S4].
No member has cosponsored the bill [S3].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name drug manufacturers: with the bill going nowhere, current US net prices on Medicare and Medicaid drugs are untouched, and nothing in the record changes what patients pay.

for.name: Rep. Daniel Meuser
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before two committees

sides.party_line_note: No one has publicly opposed the bill in the record, but no one has joined the sponsor either — it has zero cosponsors and no committee action, so no partisan divide has been drawn.

industries.note: Under the mandatory model, these companies would collect substantially lower net prices on covered drugs sold to Medicare and Medicaid patients. Their off-ramps — negotiating a covered agreement or triggering a suspension — still require providing MFN price access, but let them bundle the concession with US manufacturing commitments and negotiate scope, which is why the industry's interest in this bill runs against the patients it would cover.

industries.industry: Hospitals and physician practices that administer Part B drugs
industries.note: These providers would buy doctor-administered drugs at the MFN price for eligible patients, cutting their acquisition costs but also shrinking the revenue margins they currently earn on the spread between what they pay and what Medicare reimburses. The net effect on any given practice depends on its drug mix.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and dual referral to Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, the bill follows the most common path in Congress: it will almost certainly sit in committee and expire at the end of the session unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support or leadership decides to prioritize it, neither of which is indicated by the record.
